title: Decision: William Thompson & Son (Dumbarton) Ltd v The Scottish Ministers
text:
LANDS TRIBUNAL FOR SCOTLAND

Citation: [2025] LTS 25 , Case reference: LTS/COMP/2024/0007

OPINION OF THE TRIBUNAL

Tribunal members: Lord Duthie , Mr C C Marwick FRICS

William Thompson & Son (Dumbarton) Ltd
Applicant
against
The Scottish Ministers
Respondents

Subjects: Sheep Hill, Auchentorlie, Old Kilpatrick, Dunbartonshire

Applicant: JDC Findlay KC; Brodies  LLP
Respondents: Mure KC; Anderson Strathern  LLP

17 December 2025

Introduction

[1] This is an application under section 7 of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act 1979. The applicant seeks compensation in respect of expenditure, loss and damage said to have been sustained in consequence of the decision of the Scottish Ministers to grant scheduled monument consent, subject to conditions, in respect of proposed quarrying operations at the subjects, which would result in the complete removal of a scheduled monument. The scheduled monument in question is a vitrified fort.

[2] The matter called before the Tribunal at a diet of debate. The Tribunal members are grateful to senior counsel for their helpful submissions, including their written submissions, which are available in the Tribunal process. The respondents challenge the relevancy of the applicant’s case, contending that the claim is excluded by the terms of section 7(3) of the 1979 Act. The applicant submits that the claim is not so excluded.

Circumstances giving rise to this application

[3] The applicant operates a whinstone quarry at the subjects. Planning permission to work the quarry was originally granted on 3 November 1949, following an appeal. In 1970, the Secretary of State for Scotland included a vitrified fort at Sheep Hill within the list of scheduled monuments. The fort lies within the boundaries of the quarry and is not accessible to the public. In 1984, Historic Scotland granted scheduled monument consent for the removal of part of the fort. In 2002, consent was granted for the complete removal of the fort, subject to a condition requiring archaeological excavation and recording. That consent lapsed in 2007. On 10 September 2021, the applicant applied to Historic Environment Scotland for scheduled monument consent to carry out quarrying operations that would result in the complete removal of the fort. The application was called in by the Scottish Ministers on 9 September 2022. Following a site visit and report by the appointed reporter, consent was granted on 31 August 2023. The consent was subject to three conditions. First, no works were to commence within the scheduled area unless and until a Written Scheme of Investigation had been submitted to and approved in writing by Historic Environment Scotland. Second, the applicant was required to secure the implementation of a programme of archaeological work and to complete a programme of archaeological survey, evaluation and excavation in accordance with the approved scheme before any other consented works took place. Completion of these archaeological works had to be confirmed in writing by Historic Environment Scotland before any other works could begin. Third, the Written Scheme of Investigation was to be fully implemented during the course of the approved works. The applicant seeks compensation in respect of the costs of complying with these conditions.

Statutory framework

[4] The 1979 Act provides, inter alia , as follows:

“ 2.— Control of works affecting scheduled monuments.

(1) If any person executes or causes or permits to be executed any works to which this section applies he shall be guilty of an offence unless the works are authorised under this Part of this Act or by development consent.

(2) This section applies to any of the following works, that is to say—

(a) any works resulting in the demolition or destruction of or any damage to a scheduled monument;

(b) any works for the purpose of removing or repairing a scheduled monument or any part of it or of making any alterations or additions thereto; and

(c) any flooding or tipping operations on land in, on or under which there is a scheduled monument.

(3) Without prejudice to any other authority to execute works conferred under this Part of this Act, works to which this section applies are authorised under this Part of this Act if—

(a) the Secretary of State or Historic Environment Scotland has granted consent (referred to below in this Act as ‘scheduled monument consent’ ) for the execution of the works; and

(b) the works are executed in accordance with the terms of the consent and of any conditions attached to the consent.

…

(6) Without prejudice to subsection (1) above, if a person executing or causing or permitting to be executed any works to which a scheduled monument consent relates fails to comply with any condition attached to the consent he shall be guilty of an offence, unless he proves that he took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence to avoid contravening the condition.

…

7.— Compensation for refusal of scheduled monument consent.

(1) Subject to the following provisions of this section, where a person who has an interest in the whole or any part of a monument incurs expenditure or otherwise sustains any loss or damage in consequence of the refusal, or the granting subject to conditions, of a scheduled monument consent in relation to any works of a description mentioned in subsection (2) below, Historic Environment Scotland or, where the Scottish Ministers refused the scheduled monument consent or granted it subject to conditions, Ministers or (where the monument in question is situated in England) the Commission shall pay to that person compensation in respect of that expenditure, loss or damage. References in this section and in section 8 of this Act to compensation being paid in respect of any works are references to compensation being paid in respect of any expenditure incurred or other loss or damage sustained in consequence of the refusal, or the granting subject to conditions, of a scheduled monument consent in relation to those works.

(2) The following are works in respect of which compensation is payable under this section—

(a) works which are reasonably necessary for carrying out any development for which planning permission had been granted (otherwise than by a general development order) before the time when the monument in question became a scheduled monument and was still effective at the date of the application for scheduled monument consent;

…

(c) works which are reasonably necessary for the continuation of any use of the monument for any purpose for which it was in use immediately before the date of the application for scheduled monument consent.

…

(3) The compensation payable under this section in respect of any works within subsection (2)(a) above shall be limited to compensation in respect of any expenditure incurred or other loss or damage sustained by virtue of the fact that, in consequence of Historic Environment Scotland's or, as the case may be, the Scottish Ministers decision, any development for which the planning permission in question was granted could not be carried out without contravening section 2(1) of this Act.

…

(5) In a case where scheduled monument consent is granted subject to conditions, a person shall not be entitled to compensation under this section by virtue of subsection (2)(c) above unless compliance with those conditions would in effect make it impossible to use the monument for the purpose there mentioned.”

Submissions for the respondents

[5] The application is irrelevant and should be dismissed. Section 7(3) of the 1979 Act limits compensation to cases where the development for which planning permission has been granted cannot be carried out without contravening section 2(1). In the present case, the development may lawfully proceed provided the conditions attached to the scheduled monument consent are complied with.

[6] Reference was made to the original planning permission granted in 1949 and the subsequent review of conditions in 2020, both of which included archaeological provisions. The conditions imposed by the Scottish Ministers do not prevent the development, rather, they regulate its execution.

[7] The policy of section 7(3) is to limit compensation to cases involving a loss of development rights. No such loss arises here. The development remains capable of lawful execution, subject to compliance with the conditions. The conditions imposed in this case require archaeological investigation and recording prior to commencement and during the course of the works. The types of expenditure, loss and damage described by the applicant are not sustained by virtue of the fact that the development cannot be carried out without contravening section 2(1). The development remains capable of lawful execution if the conditions are met. The claim is therefore excluded by section 7(3).

[8] Senior counsel referred to The Law of Compulsory Purchase , Honey KC et al, 5 th edition, 2025 at [386]:

“Where the claim relates to works necessary for carrying out development, compensation can only relate to loss sustained by virtue of the fact that any development for which planning permission has been granted could not be carried out without infringing the requirement for consent”;

and to Listed Buildings and Other Heritage Assets, Mynors & Hewitson, 6 th edition, 2024 at 14-30:

“Where scheduled monument consent is refused, or granted subject to onerous conditions, there is a very limited right to compensation, under section 7 of the Ancient Monuments Act or section 21 of the HE (Wales) Act”.

Submissions for the applicant

[9] The applicant has stated a relevant claim under section 7(2)(a) of the 1979 Act. Planning permission for the proposed development was granted on 3 November 1949, prior to the scheduling of the monument in 1970. Scheduled monument consent was granted on 31 August 2023, subject to three conditions. Section 2(3) provides that works are authorised only if executed in accordance with the terms of the consent and any conditions attached thereto. Failure to comply with the conditions would result in a contravention of section 2(1). The development cannot lawfully proceed unless the conditions are fulfilled.

[10] The applicant’s claim for compensation is not excluded by section 7(3). Had Parliament intended to restrict or exclude compensation for the costs of complying with conditions in respect of works falling within section 7(2)(a), it would have done so expressly, as it did in section 7(5) in respect of works falling within section 7(2)(c). However, Parliament did not do that. Instead, section 7(3) limits compensation in respect of works falling within section 7(2)(a) to expenditure incurred or loss sustained by virtue of the fact that the development cannot be lawfully carried out without contravening section 2(1).

[11] Compensation is available in respect of expenditure required to comply with conditions attached to scheduled monument consent, where such compliance is necessary to avoid contravention of section 2(1). Where works are carried out in compliance with conditions attached to scheduled monument consent, and thereby do not contravene section 2(1), the associated expenditure is not excluded by section 7(3). Section 7(3) excludes compensation for consequential costs arising from the imposition of conditions, but not for expenditure necessary to ensure that the development proceeds lawfully.

[12] Compliance with the conditions will require significant expenditure, both now and in the future. That expenditure arises by virtue of the statutory prohibition in section 2(1) and is therefore not excluded by section 7(3). The conditions are integral to the authorisation and must be purified before the development can lawfully commence. Reference was made to Whitley & Sons v Secretary of State for Wales and Clywd County Council 64 P & C R 296, a planning law case, where Woolf LJ stated:

“The permission is controlled by and subject to the conditions. If the operations contravene the conditions they cannot be properly described as commencing the development authorised by the permission. If they do not comply with the permission they constitute a breach of planning control and for planning purposes will be unauthorised and thus unlawful.”

The same principle applies to scheduled monument consent. Compliance is not optional, rather, a prerequisite to legality. The costs of ensuring legality are accordingly within the contemplation of section 7(3). The Tribunal should allow an evidential hearing.

The competing interpretations of section 7(3)

[13] Section 7(1) creates a right to compensation in respect of the three categories of works set out in section 7(2) for expenditure incurred and loss or damage sustained in consequence of the refusal or the granting subject to conditions of a scheduled monument consent. The instant application relates to works under section 7(2)(a), as the planning permission predates the scheduling of the monument.

[14] Section 7(3) limits compensation for section 7(2)(a) works to expenditure or loss sustained by virtue of the fact that, in consequence of the decision, any development for which the planning permission in question was granted could not be carried out without contravening section 2(1). The narrow issue of statutory interpretation arising is whether that statutory phrase refers only to absolute prohibitions on development or whether it encompasses also conditional prohibitions, where a development cannot lawfully proceed unless the conditions attached to the relative scheduled monument consent are fulfilled.

[15] We have not found discerning Parliament’s intention in respect of section 7(3) straightforward. Section 7(1) creates a general right to compensation. Section 7(3) and section 7(5) then qualify that right for specific categories of works, but use materially different language for each qualification.

[16] The phrase “could not be carried out without contravening section 2(1)” admits of two possible readings. On the narrower reading commended by the respondents, it focuses on whether there exists any lawful route to carry out the development. On arguably the more purposive interpretation commended by the applicant, it treats conditions as integral to authorisation so that, until they are satisfied, the prohibition in section 2(1) remains operative. Both readings have merit.

Legislative intent

[17] Given the competing interpretations of section 7(3) commended by parties, we considered it permissible (see Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593 per Lord Browne Wilkinson at page 640 D to H) to consult ministerial statements as recorded in Hansard in the hope of better understanding the legislative intent.

[18] During the passage of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Bill, Ministers explained that clause 7 was intended to provide a limited right to compensation where scheduled monument consent was refused or granted subject to conditions, in order to strike a fair balance between heritage protection and the legitimate expectations of landowners. In the House of Commons, Mr Kenneth Marks, Under‑Secretary of State for the Environment, stated that the Bill:

“strikes an acceptable balance between the need to preserve, or at least to record, our heritage and the requirements of developers, landowners, farmers, mineral operators and others whose business must inevitably involve a measure of archaeological damage” (HC Deb. 4 April 1979, vol 965, col 1360).

In the House of Lords, Baroness Stedman, Under‑Secretary of State for the Environment, explained that conditions attached to scheduled monument consent were integral to the statutory scheme and necessary to ensure archaeological recording before works proceed, stating:

“it is Clause 7 which makes the provision for compensation for the refusal of monument consent or for conditions imposed on the consent. Then, if we go on to Clause 9, that provides for compensation where consent has been given and has been subsequently revoked or modified. The compensation is meant to cover abortive expenditure and other loss or damage that is directly attributable to the revocation or modification of the consent” (HL Deb 20 February 1979, vol 398, col 1740).

[19] Neither statement deals specifically with section 7(3), although they do tend to confirm that Parliament envisaged conditions as part of authorisation and contemplated compensation where conditions imposed under clause 7 created financial burdens. That does not assist much beyond paraphrasing the wording of the Act. There is no express suggestion of an intention to confine relief to cases of absolute prohibition but equally there is no express statement that compliance costs are recoverable in respect of section 7(2)(a) works. The statements in Parliament confirm the general policy but do not assist resolve the ambiguity in section 7(3).

The respondents’ proposed construction

[20] The respondents advance a narrow construction of section 7(3). On this view, the phrase “could not be carried out without contravening subsection 2(1)” is concerned solely with whether the carrying out of the development would be unlawful in the sense that no lawful path exists to proceed. Conditions regulate the manner and timing of execution. They do not extinguish the development right. If the conditions are capable of being fulfilled and, once fulfilled, the development can lawfully proceed, then the development could be carried out without contravening section 2(1). The existence of compliance costs does not convert a conditional authorisation into a prohibition.

[21] This construction holds that section 7(3) is a targeted limitation on what is recoverable for the category of works in section 7(2)(a). It confines compensation to loss arising from the development becoming unlawful. It does not extend to costs of lawful compliance. This reading is said to be supported by the structure of section 7. Parliament expressly stipulated in section 7(5) that a person is not entitled to compensation for works within section 7(2)(c), unless compliance with conditions would in effect make it impossible to use the monument for the relevant purpose. Parliament chose different words in section 7(3). It did not refer to conditions. It referred instead to unlawfulness (“contravening section 2(1)”). The distinction is said to be deliberate and the consequence that compliance costs for section 7(2)(a) works are excluded from what is recoverable under the scheme.

[22] Such a construction promotes clarity and certainty. It avoids open ended claims for compliance costs that may be variable and project specific. It reflects the limited nature of the statutory compensation regime and respects the policy of the Act by ensuring that conditions which secure archaeological investigation and recording are not discouraged by financial liability. On this view loss of development rights is compensable but compliance costs are the price of authorisation and fall on the developer.

[23] Such a construction finds support in the commentaries referred to by senior counsel for the respondents. This construction has both simplicity and logic. Were this interpretation to be preferred, the applicant’s claim would fail because the development remains capable of lawful execution if conditions are met. Unlawfulness is avoided by compliance.

The applicant’s proposed construction

[24] The applicant commends a construction whereby conditions are integral to authorisation by virtue of section 2(3) and section 2(6). Until conditions are satisfied, the prohibition in section 2(1) remains operative. The development could not lawfully be carried out without contravening section 2(1) unless those conditions are fulfilled. Expenditure necessary to purify conditions is said to be expenditure sustained by virtue of the statutory prohibition and therefore not excluded by section 7(3).

[25] This construction, it is said, best accords with the scheme and purpose of section 7. Section 7(2)(a) protects development rights conferred before scheduling. To exclude compliance costs would be to undermine that protection in a manner that is arbitrary. When Parliament intended to restrict compensation by reference to conditions it did so expressly in section 7(5) in relation to section 7(2)(c) works. The absence of comparable language in section 7(3), senior counsel submitted, is telling.

Decision

[26] The applicant’s claim is excluded by section 7(3) of the 1979 Act.

[27] The applicant seeks compensation in respect of expenditure said to have been sustained in consequence of the decision of the Scottish Ministers to grant scheduled monument consent, subject to conditions. The application accordingly falls within the scope of section 7(2)(a). Those conditions must be fulfilled before the development can lawfully proceed. The conditions require a Written Scheme of Investigation, the completion and confirmation of archaeological works, and the implementation of the scheme during the course of the works. These conditions regulate the manner in which the development may proceed. They do not render the development unlawful.

[28] Whether or not Parliament intended to exclude compensation in respect of compliance costs for section 7(2)(a) works - and even if that effect might have been achieved by a different legislative approach - that is what section 7(3) does. Section 7(3), as framed, is concerned with the existence of a lawful path to carry out the development, not with the cost of walking that path. It poses the simple question: could the development be carried out without contravening section 2(1)? Where scheduled monument consent has been granted subject to conditions, the development is capable of lawful execution. Unlawfulness is avoided by compliance.

[29] The applicant’s claim for compensation in respect of compliance costs accordingly does not fall within the scope of permissible claims under section 7(3). Compensation is only available in respect of section 7(2)(a) works where the decision has the effect that the development cannot lawfully be carried out at all. To read into section 7(3) a right to recover all expenditure necessary to avoid contravention would be to stretch the wording of section 7(3) to breaking point.

[30] We recognise that the applicant’s construction is not without merit. It draws attention to the integral role of conditions within section 2 and to the policy objective of protecting development rights conferred before scheduling. These considerations have force. However, in our view they cannot overcome the constraints of the statutory language. Section 7(3) does not refer to conditions or to compliance costs. To adopt the applicant’s interpretation would require us to read words into the provision that Parliament did not include by adding, at the end of section 7(3), the gloss averred by the applicant at paragraph 3.12 of the adjusted application (“unless the conditions applied to the scheduled monument are complied with”). It is not permissible to rewrite section 7(3) under the pretext of interpretation.

[31] The architecture of section 7 supports this conclusion. Section 7(1) creates a general right to compensation. As noted above, section 7(3) and section 7(5) then qualify that right for specific categories of works using different language appropriate to each context. Section 7(5) addresses paragraph (c) works and expressly ties entitlement to the effect of conditions making it impossible to use the monument for the relevant purpose. Section 7(3) addresses paragraph (a) works and ties entitlement to unlawfulness. The deliberate choice of different formulations indicates different thresholds. If Parliament had intended conditions to be the touchstone for paragraph (a) works it could have said so, as it did for paragraph (c). Parliament did not do so.

[32] The authorities and commentaries cited by the respondents are eloquent of the limited nature of compensation in this area. While compliance with conditions attached to scheduled monument consent is necessary for lawfulness, it does not follow that the cost of achieving compliance is itself a loss sustained by virtue of the fact that development could not be carried out. Here the proposed development can be carried out lawfully by complying with conditions.

[33] Although nothing turns on it, this interpretation has practical virtues. It promotes clarity and certainty. It aligns better with the limited nature of the statutory scheme. It confines compensation under section 7(3) to situations where development is truly barred. It avoids open‑ended and variable claims for compliance costs. It respects the policy of the Act by ensuring that conditions securing archaeological investigation and recording are not discouraged by financial liability absent a clear legislative mandate.

Disposal

[34] Section 7(3) operates to exclude the applicant’s claim. The application is irrelevant. On the respondents’ motion, we dismiss the application.

[35] We appoint parties to enrol any motions for expenses within 21 days of the date of notification of this decision. If any such motion is opposed parties should confirm whether they are content for the question of expenses to be determined on the basis of written submissions in accordance with the Tribunal’s normal practice.
